newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian lawmakers vote to bankrupt drug barons.
newsitem.headline: Colombian lawmakers vote to bankrupt drug barons.

text.p: Lawmakers have taken the first step towards passing legislation that would bankrupt some of the world's richest criminals by allowing the government to seize assets linked to Colombia 's lucrative drug trade.
The so-called asset forfeiture law, aimed at cracking down on the drug-related crime of "illicit enrichment," was approved by two committees meeting jointly late on Thursday after weeks of debate.

The plenaries of the House of Representatives and Senate will open debate over the asset forfeiture bill next week. If passed, it would be signed into law by Samper on December 16 when the current session of Congress closes.
The legislation was proposed more than three months ago by President Ernesto Samper, under heavy U.S. pressure to demonstrate his government's commitment to the global struggle against narcotics.

The bill, approved 27-21 by a joint session of the constitutional committees of the Senate and House, would allow the government to seize the bank accounts, palatial homes, sports cars and yachts of any convicted drug trafficker or individual -- including several jailed Colombian congressmen -- who benefitted from the drug trade.
Estimates varied as to how much money could be turned over to the state but some traffickers, including jailed leaders of the Cali drug mob, amassed personal fortunes said to total up to $12 billion.

Colombia, the world's top producer of cocaine and a leading supplier of heroin to the United States, was decertified as a full-fledged partner in the U.S. drug war last March because of Samper's alleged ties to drug traffickers charged with pouring millions of dollars into his 1994 election campaign.
U.S. officials said Washington would seek to cripple Colombia's economy unless Samper bowed to demands for stiffer penalities against drug trafficking.
Numerous death threats were reported against congressmen supporting the measures.

The thorniest issue, and focal point of hours of heated debate, was the government's insistence that asset forfeiture take effect retroactively -- from 1974 when drug trafficking officially became a crime in Colombia, and 1989, when illicit enrichment was introduced into the country's penal code.
